title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Radial keratotomy is one of the earliest, most widely adopted refractive surgical procedures for correcting myopia. The technique achieves refractive change by flattening the central cornea through deep radial stromal incisions, reducing excessive corneal curvature. Radial keratotomy was most commonly performed in young adults with low-to-moderate myopia before the advent of excimer laser–based refractive surgery. Although use has declined substantially, a large population of individuals with prior radial keratotomy continues to present for care. Long-term sequelae include fluctuating vision, progressive hyperopic shift, glare, halos, and reduced visual quality, particularly under mesopic conditions. Management of post–radial keratotomy refractive error requires careful diagnostic evaluation, recognition of altered corneal biomechanics, and consideration of refractive unpredictability. Indications for intervention include visually significant refractive error or optical aberrations, whereas corneal fragility and active ocular disease represent important contraindications.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This educational activity enhances clinician competence in evaluating and managing patients with prior radial keratotomy. Participants gain an improved understanding of corneal anatomy, incision biomechanics, and wound-healing responses relevant to long-term outcomes. Instruction emphasizes appropriate candidate selection, interpretation of corneal topography, and strategies for managing refractive instability and visual aberrations. Learners develop skills necessary to anticipate procedural challenges, including biometry limitations and surgical risk associated with prior incisions. Collaboration with an interprofessional team, including optometrists, ophthalmic technicians, and surgical staff, strengthens diagnostic accuracy, supports perioperative planning, and promotes individualized care, thereby improving long-term visual outcomes and patient safety.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify clinical and diagnostic features suggestive of complications following radial keratotomy. Select appropriate interventions for the treatment of complications following radial keratotomy. Improve patient awareness of postoperative care, visual fluctuations, potential complications, and the importance of regular follow-up to optimize long-term outcomes after radial keratotomy. Collaborate with all members of the interprofessional team to improve coordinated care and outcomes in patients who have undergone radial keratotomy and require correction. title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Introduction
content: Refractive surgery is a laser procedure performed to alter the eye’s refractive power and reduce dependence on spectacles and contact lenses. Radial keratotomy was among the first and most widely performed refractive surgical procedures of the 20th century. Approximately 10% of practicing ophthalmologists in the United States (US) have performed several hundred thousand radial keratotomy procedures. Lans demonstrated in the late 19th century that deep radial incisions in the anterior cornea caused central corneal flattening with peripheral steepening. Sato later performed posterior radial keratotomy in 8 patients with keratoconus in the 1930s. [1] [2] Enhanced flattening resulted from longer and deeper incisions. Although initially effective, the Sato technique ultimately produced bullous keratopathy in up to 70% of patients due to endothelial damage. [3]

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Introduction
content: Improvements to the radial keratotomy procedure, restricting incisions solely to the anterior corneal surface, were undertaken in the 1970s in Russia. The use of multifactorial formulae and nomograms, incorporating both patient and surgical variables, improved predictive performance. [4] [5] [6] Radial keratotomy correction was introduced to the US in 1978 by Bores et al, Myers, and Cowden, with multiple surgeons performing procedures and publishing anecdotal results. [7] [8] [9] [10] Early publications were optimistic, and reported complications were few. These observations prompted the National Institutes of Health to fund the Prospective Evaluation of Radial Keratotomy (PERK) study, which assessed the safety, efficacy, stability, and predictability of the technique.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Introduction
content: The PERK study involved 12 surgeons practicing at 9 clinical centers, who performed radial keratotomy on 793 eyes of 435 patients with myopia ranging from 2 to 8 diopters. [11] Technique refinements and improvements continued following the PERK study. Younger individuals exhibit greater rates and extent of wound healing, requiring more extensive surgery to achieve equivalent outcomes compared with older individuals. Advances in surgical equipment, including diamond blades and ultrasonic pachymeter calibration, further improved procedural predictability. With the introduction of more accurate and stable laser refractive surgery, ie, photorefractive keratectomy (PRK), laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), small incision lenticule extraction (SMILE), and intraocular lens (IOL) surgery, the popularity of radial keratotomy correction has decreased considerably. However, given the large number of patients who have undergone this procedure, knowledge of radial keratotomy and its variants remains essential for managing cases requiring subsequent visual rehabilitation.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The eye functions as a compound optical system, comprising a cornea and a lens component. The total refracting power of the normal eye is approximately 64 D, with the cornea contributing approximately two-thirds, or 43 D. The anterior and posterior corneal surfaces, along with the crystalline lens, focus incident light rays onto the retina. In an emmetropic eye, light rays from infinity are focused precisely on the retina, with the dioptric power of the eye matching its axial length, producing in-focus images. In ametropic eyes, axial length deviations or corneal/lenticular astigmatism prevent light rays from converging on the retina, resulting in blurred or defocused images.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The normal cornea is a transparent, avascular structure with a convex shape. The average diameter measures 11.5 mm, and the thickness increases from 550 to 565 μm centrally to 610 to 640 μm peripherally. [12] Dense innervation is supplied by long ciliary nerves originating from the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V1). [13] The cornea consists of multiple layers: the epithelium, Bowman layer, stroma, pre-Descemet (Dua) layer, Descemet layer, and endothelium. The corneal epithelium serves as the primary barrier to the external environment, while the tear film provides a smooth optical surface. The central epithelium contains 5 to 7 cellular layers, whereas the periphery contains 7 to 10 layers. Average epithelial thickness is 50 μm. When epithelial defects occur, such as corneal abrasions, limbal stem cells proliferate in the periphery and migrate to the defect site to replace lost cells. [14]

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The Bowman layer, also known as the anterior limiting lamina, forms the most anterior aspect of the corneal stroma and comprises 8 to 12 μm of densely arranged, mainly type I collagen fibrils. This layer thins with aging, and histopathological changes have been documented in individuals with keratoconus. [15] The corneal stroma provides mechanical strength and consists of collagen fibers, interconnected keratocytes, and glycosaminoglycans arranged in regular, densely packed lamellae. In the central cornea, lamellae exhibit higher anterior density compared with the posterior. Incisional procedures, such as radial keratotomy, disrupt the stroma and permanently reduce corneal mechanical strength (see Images . Sixteen-Incision Radial Keratotomy in the Left Eye; Standard 8-Incision Radial Keratotomy with Sparing of the Pupillary Zone).

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The Descemet membrane is a basement membrane measuring 5 to 10 μm and is divided into anterior and posterior layers. The posterior layer is produced by endothelial cells and increases in thickness with advancing age. [16] The corneal endothelium forms a single layer of cells on the most posterior corneal surface. This layer maintains osmotic balance, preventing corneal edema and loss of transparency. Endothelial cells are nonregenerative, and their density declines steadily with age. [17] Radial keratotomy alters the refractive power of the anterior corneal surface by creating individual linear incisions that extend approximately 80% to 90% of the stromal depth. The number of incisions ranges from 4 to 24, with 8 being most commonly used. [18] Surgical outcomes are influenced by incision length, depth, and number, as well as patient factors such as sex and age.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Indications
content: Radial keratotomy correction is indicated for patients with moderate myopia. Candidates should be at least 18 years old to ensure stable refraction and the ability to provide informed consent for surgery. Individuals wearing contact lenses must discontinue using these corrective devices and undergo multiple serial corneal topography scans and cycloplegic refractions to confirm refractive stability prior to surgery.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Contraindications -- Absolute Contraindications
content: Contraindications to radial keratotomy are similar to those for other types of refractive surgical correction. Absolute contraindications include refractive instability, defined as changes greater than 0.5 D within the previous 12 months. Systemic conditions that can produce refractive instability include pregnancy and uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Contraindications -- Absolute Contraindications
content: Patients with unstable collagen vascular diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren syndrome, Graves disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease, are at increased risk of ocular conditions that directly affect vision or impair wound healing, including keratoconjunctivitis sicca. [19] Corneal ectasia may occur postoperatively if the cornea is mechanically weak. Therefore, patients with keratoconus or thin corneas, defined as less than 500 μm centrally, are not suitable candidates for surgery. Active ocular surface infection, such as keratitis, or ongoing inflammation, may worsen with surgical intervention. These conditions constitute a contraindication to proceeding with radial keratotomy.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Contraindications -- Relative Contraindications
content: Relative contraindications to radial keratotomy vary with individual patient characteristics. Advancing age may be associated with cataract development, which can reduce visual acuity despite radial keratotomy correction. Cataract surgery with IOL implantation may provide superior improvement in unaided distance visual acuity for these patients.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Contraindications -- Relative Contraindications
content: Coexisting corneal pathology, such as scarring, corneal dystrophy, or herpetic eye disease, can limit the degree of visual improvement and increase the risk of visual loss. Larger pupil diameter may exacerbate postsurgical visual symptoms, including glare and halos, particularly under low-light conditions. [20] Normal adult pupil diameter ranges from 2 to 4 mm in bright light and 4 to 8 mm in darkness, with physiological anisocoria of up to 1 mm considered normal. Radial keratotomy is a relative contraindication in patients with glaucoma who require regular intraocular pressure (IOP) monitoring (normal range: 10–21 mm Hg), as altered corneal biomechanical properties may lead to underestimation of measured IOP. [21]

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Equipment
content: Equipment required for performing radial keratotomy includes topical anesthetic eye drops, gentian ink for corneal marking, an optical zone marker, a corneal incision marker, and an ultrasonic pachymeter. A gem-quality diamond blade knife with a 45° cutting angle, along with postoperative antibiotic and steroid eye drops, is also necessary.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Personnel
content: An interprofessional care team for radial keratotomy includes ophthalmic surgeons, optometrists, ophthalmic nurses and assistants, theatre staff, orthoptists, imaging technicians, and medical assistants. Coordination among these team members ensures safe, efficient procedural performance and optimal patient outcomes.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Preparation
content: A thorough history and clinical examination are required to identify potential contraindications to radial keratotomy. Occupational history should be obtained, and the patient’s visual goals and expectations assessed. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the ocular surface includes evaluation for dry eye, measurement of IOP, corneal assessment, determination of cataract status, and dilated fundoscopic examination. Contact lenses must be discontinued 1 to 2 weeks prior to corneal imaging to ensure accurate measurements. [22] Corneal evaluation with keratometry, topography, and ultrasound pachymetry constitutes standard preoperative practice.

content: Equipment must be checked for safety, and all patient data should be verified by clinical staff to minimize the risk of errors. Informed written consent is obtained prior to the day of the procedure, allowing sufficient time to address questions and concerns.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Technique or Treatment -- Surgical Technique
content: The basic elements of radial keratotomy are deceptively simple and include administration of appropriate anesthesia; accurate marking of the visual axis and incision lines, accounting for cyclotorsion; measurement of corneal thickness; precise adjustment of blade depth; creation of corneal incisions; and administration of postoperative antibiotic drops. Topical anesthesia is used in most patients to allow ocular mobility for accurate visual axis marking. The size of the optical zone is determined by the surgeon's preference. In the PERK study, the clear central zone was defined as a spherical-equivalent cycloplegic refraction of 3 to 4 mm.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Technique or Treatment -- Surgical Technique
content: Corneal thickness was measured at 4 paracentral points within the defined optical zone in each quadrant, with an average of 3 readings taken to maximize accuracy. The diamond knife is set to the appropriate depth based on pachymetric measurements, and 8 incisions are typically made; fewer incisions are used for lower degrees of myopia. Additional incisions may be considered in cases of postoperative undercorrection. Radial incisions correct myopia, whereas hexagonal incisions, known as hexagonal keratotomy, address hyperopia. [23] Variations in incision technique, including the point of initiation, direction, depth, and length, have been proposed to improve outcomes and long-term refractive stability. [24] [25]

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Technique or Treatment -- Postoperative Measures
content: Postoperative eye drops were not routinely prescribed during the early years of radial keratotomy, contributing to the procedure’s popularity. Subsequent use of topical steroids aimed to enhance the radial keratotomy effect by modulating wound healing. Dry eye symptoms are managed with topical ocular lubricants. Long-term follow-up with the surgeon is essential, as studies' results have confirmed that achieving stable refraction and maintaining visual quality remain challenges in patients who have undergone radial keratotomy

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Technique or Treatment -- Alternative Corneal Incisional Surgery
content: Astigmatic keratotomy, also known as arcuate keratotomy, involves placing deep corneal incisions along the steep axis of astigmatism, thereby flattening the targeted meridian. A coupling effect occurs, resulting in the steepening of the opposite, perpendicular meridian. [26] The relationship between flattening in the incised meridian and steepening in the perpendicular meridian is defined as the coupling ratio, which is typically 1. [27] Incision depth reaches approximately 95% of the midperipheral corneal thickness.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Technique or Treatment -- Alternative Corneal Incisional Surgery
content: Astigmatic keratotomy has been employed after cataract surgery and following penetrating keratoplasty to manage residual astigmatism. [28] [29] Limbal relaxing incisions are created at 50 μm less than the thinnest measured pachymetry at the corneal limbus and represent an alternative method for astigmatism management during cataract surgery. [30] Modern refinements include the use of femtosecond lasers and nomograms to improve the precision and reproducibility of these incisions. [31] [32]

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Complications -- Sight-Threatening Sequelae
content: Complications have been reported in 1% to 3% of eyes. Bacterial and fungal keratitis, as well as endophthalmitis, have occurred following radial keratotomy. [33] [34] [35] Inadvertent full-thickness incisions can result in intraoperative trauma, cataract formation, and hemorrhage. [36] Reduced biomechanical stability at incision sites may predispose the globe to rupture through keratotomy scars. [37] In the PERK study, 3% of eyes lost 2 or more lines of best-corrected visual acuity. [38]

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Complications -- Non-Sight-Threatening Complications
content: Dry eye may develop following radial keratotomy due to reduced tear production. Nerve damage from corneal incisions disrupts the lacrimal reflex and interferes with the tear production cycle. Visual aberrations, including halos, glare, light-bursts around lights, haze, and decreased contrast sensitivity, can occur after radial keratotomy. Higher-order aberrations and increased pupil size are associated with the procedure. [39]

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Complications -- Non-Sight-Threatening Complications
content: Long-term follow-up has demonstrated hyperopic regression 10 years after radial keratotomy. [40] Approximately 22% of eyes drifted 1 D or more toward hyperopia, and 2% drifted 1 D or more toward myopia, between 6 months and 5 years postoperatively, in the PERK study. Diurnal variation in visual acuity, refraction, and corneal topographic indices has also been reported 10 years after surgery. [41]

Diurnal variation in visual acuity, refraction, and corneal topographic indices has also been reported 10 years after surgery. [41]

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Complications -- Cataract Surgery in Patients with Previous Radial Keratotomy
content: Cataract surgery in individuals with a history of radial keratotomy presents unique challenges due to altered corneal biomechanics and irregular refractive outcomes. [42] Accurate IOL power calculation is difficult because radial keratotomy flattens the central cornea and distorts keratometry. Modern formulas, historical refractive data, and tomography-based measurements improve calculation accuracy, although variability persists. [43] [44] [45] Surgeons should anticipate refractive surprises, consider targeting mild myopia, and provide counseling regarding potential postoperative instability. [46] [47] Intraoperative aberrometry may assist in IOL selection. The surgical technique is generally routine, but care is required to avoid intersecting previous radial keratotomy incisions, which increases the risk of wound dehiscence and corneal instability.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Clinical Significance
content: Individuals who have undergone radial keratotomy correction are at risk for both sight-threatening and non-sight-threatening complications in the short and long term. Visual quality may fluctuate throughout the day, and hyperopic regression occurs over time. The development of presbyopia and cataract further complicates visual rehabilitation in this population. Methods for improving IOL power calculations in eyes with prior radial keratotomy have been described. [48]

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Clinical Significance
content: A modern iteration of radial keratotomy includes asymmetric mini–radial keratotomy as part of treatment protocols for keratoconus. [49] Considerations include the underlying biomechanical stability of the cornea, which influences measurement accuracy, the presence of irregular astigmatism, the size of the optical zone, and the location of incisions. Significant corneal instability, irregularity, or scarring may necessitate initial collagen crosslinking, with or without therapeutic excimer laser ablation for scar removal, to facilitate accurate biometry measurements.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Radial keratotomy was an early surgical procedure designed to correct myopia by creating deep corneal incisions that alter anterior corneal curvature. Although largely replaced by modern laser-based techniques such as LASIK, PRK, SMILE, and IOL surgery, many individuals who underwent radial keratotomy correction in the 1980s and 1990s now experience long-term complications, such as progressive hyperopic shift, diurnal visual fluctuations, irregular astigmatism, and challenges with IOL calculations during cataract surgery. Knowledge of corneal anatomy, biomechanics, and refractive stability is essential for safe and effective management, as corneas previously subjected to radial keratotomy exhibit altered structural properties that increase the risk of visual instability and surgical complications.

title: Radial Keratotomy Correction -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Proficiency in evidence-based diagnostic tools, including corneal topography and pachymetry, and in strategies for visual rehabilitation and patient counseling, is critical. Effective treatment of patients with prior radial keratotomy requires coordinated interprofessional care. Physicians and advanced practitioners must evaluate refractive stability, anticipate surgical risks, and develop individualized treatment plans. Nurses and technicians support patient education, preoperative preparation, and ongoing monitoring, while pharmacists optimize ocular medication management. Clear communication among team members ensures realistic patient expectations and the safe, timely delivery of interventions. Collaborative strategies and shared expertise enhance patient-centered outcomes, optimize long-term visual function, and uphold high standards of safety and clinical performance.

content: Interprofessional team members provide patient education regarding the radial keratotomy procedure and obtain informed consent prior to surgery.
